evidence: Liv. 40.5: ex quō obses Rōmae fuit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: “From the time when”. For a time that runs on into the present, Latin uses the present with jam where English says “have been”: jam diū ignōrō, “I have not known for a long time”.

terms.grammar: conjunction, with the indicative: annī sunt octō cum …
evidence: Cic. Clu. 82: annī sunt octō cum ista causa in istā meditātiōne versātur (Lewis & Short)
Plaut. Aul. prol. 4: hanc domum jam multōs annōs est quom possideō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: “It is eight years since …”, with the present when the thing still goes on.

evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.9.1: jam diū ignōrō quid agās
terms.comment: The usual Latin for “I have been … for so long”.

phrases.english: ever since he was a hostage in Rome

phrases.latin: hanc domum jam multōs annōs est quom possideō
phrases.english: it is many years now that I have owned this house

phrases.latin: jam diū ignōrō quid agās; nihil enim scrībis
phrases.english: I haven’t known for a long time how you are, for you never write

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
